Chapter 39

Remote functions: query, batch, form and command

Four kinds, one rule for choosing between them, two mistakes that both render a 500 page over a working form, and the two shapes a refusal arrives in.

By the end of this chapter

Call the server without writing an endpoint, and know which kind each call should be.

A query is a read. The interesting thing about this one is what it does *twice*: it parses and checks the query text, even though the editor already did.

Not redundancy for its own sake. The editor’s copy exists to draw a squiggle as somebody types; this one exists because the query text arrives in a URL that anybody can edit. A checker that only runs in the browser is a suggestion.

query.batch, and a resolver that returns a function

A results table of forty rows wants a small chart per row, and forty separate calls is forty round trips — on a connection with 80ms of latency that is three seconds of staircase before the last chart appears.

The subtlety worth knowing is in the last paragraph: the resolver must return a function, not an array. Returning an array makes the mapping positional, and positional mapping breaks the moment the resolver deduplicates — which it must, because a table with the same service twice would otherwise ask for it twice.

form or command: the rule

command is a function call over the network: it needs JavaScript, and if the bundle has not loaded, nothing happens. form is a real <form> that posts, progressively enhanced when the bundle is there. The rule is what the action costs when it silently does nothing. For "save this alert rule", the cost is somebody believing they are covered when they are not — so it is a form. For an enable/disable toggle that is instant, reversible and visibly reflected, a command.

Fields come from the form, not from a name attribute

What the spread buys is worth the ceremony: the field carries its own aria-invalid, its value survives a failed submission without a re-render, and a rename in the valibot schema becomes a type error here rather than a form that silently posts a key the server ignores.

defaultValue, because a remote form resets itself

A remote form resets after a successful submission — and a reset does not restore what is *selected*, it restores what each option says is its default: option.defaultSelected, which is the selected attribute. fields.as('select', …) sets the select’s value property and marks no option at all, so before this line every option’s default was false and a reset fell to the first one.

Editing a rule that fires below a threshold, saving it, and being left looking at above — a different rule, with the form still looking filled in. defaultValue on <select>, added in Svelte 5.57, is the reset target stated next to the value, and the test above exists so that deleting it fails rather than passing quietly.

And invalid, not error

error(400, …) inside a form handler throws an HttpError, which SvelteKit turns into a 500 error page — the whole form, and the list around it, replaced by "Internal Error". invalid(issue.query(…)) puts the message beside the field and marks the input. Both of these mistakes were found by one end-to-end test that creates a rule; both looked perfectly reasonable in review.

One instance per row

A remote form is a single object with one attached <form> element, so spreading the same one inside an {#each} throws — and the page then renders its error branch, which looks like the query failed rather than like a markup mistake. .for(id) mints one instance per id, which is also what gives each row its own pending state.

A command the server refuses

The toggle used to call toggleRule(…) and forget it. When the server refused, nothing said so: the rejection went unhandled, and the box went on showing what had been asked for rather than what the server had kept. A boundary could not have helped. The Svelte documentation is plain that errors “in event handlers or after a setTimeout or async work” are not caught by error boundaries. So the page catches the rejection itself, puts the box back, and shows the refusal in the row.

The line that matters is the one that reads the message, because a refusal reaches the browser in two shapes. A failed snippet is handed what SvelteKit’s handleError made of the error, and the documentation says so in a comment on its own example: “error went through the handleError hook and is of type App.Error” — { status, message }, plus whatever the app adds. Awaiting a command hands back something else: the HttpError the client rebuilt from the response, with the message on body and none of its own. A probe that ended the session under a live page, then made a list reload and pressed the toggle, printed both.

So a boundary reads message, a command’s catch reads body.message, and each is the wrong field for the other: the wrong one is undefined, and a fallback sentence quietly takes its place. isHttpError tells a refusal from a request that never reached the server, which is the one case the fallback here is for. Server code is unchanged by any of this. A remote function or a hook that catches an error() holds the HttpError itself, and isHttpError(e) && e.body.message is still right there.

The documentation writes the snippet as failed(error: App.Error). Svelte types a boundary’s failed as Snippet<[error: unknown, reset: () => void]>, so svelte-check refuses that annotation — “Type unknown is not assignable to type Error” — and the snippets here take error untyped and cast it where they read it: (error as App.Error).message.

What a boundary can catch

The explore page puts its results in one <svelte:boundary>, and the comment above it promised that a refused query — a 400 from the checker is the common case — would be explained by the boundary’s failed snippet. It never was. Pressing Run on from logs | where replaced the whole page with SvelteKit’s error page: a “400” heading, “Expected a value” under it, and no editor to fix the query in.

Two rules decide where a failure lands, one for the browser and one for the server, and the page had broken both. The browser’s rule is about where a value is *read*. The server’s is about where an await is *written*.

In the browser: thrown where it is read

An awaited value that rejects keeps the rejection as its value, and reading it throws. Read in the markup inside a boundary, it throws there, and “errors in await expressions will bubble to the nearest error boundary” means that one. A $derived that throws is the exception that caught the explore page out: Svelte computes a derived on behalf of the component that *declared* it, so what it throws is reported to the boundary around the declaration, not to the one around whatever read it.

The page declared three values made from the result — the rows, the columns and the chart — as $deriveds in its script. When the query was refused, each one threw as it read the result, and each reported from the script: to the boundary SvelteKit puts around every page, whose failed is the error page. The traces page shows the other half of the rule. It awaited its query in the script too, but only its markup read the result, inside its boundary, so in the browser its refusal was caught where it was read — the boundary (traces list) line in the probe output above is exactly that. Its trouble was on the server.

Declaration tags fix it without changing a line that uses the three. Declared inside the boundary, they report to it. The chart became a plain function, chartOf(), so that its $derived could be declared here with the other two.

On the server: every await in a script comes first

That made Run work, and a review found the other half the same day. A link to the same query still opened on the error page, and so did a reload after a refused Run, because Run writes the query into the address bar. The query itself was still awaited in the script, as const result = $derived(await runQuery(…)), and the Svelte documentation says what the server does with that: “All await expressions encountered outside boundaries with pending snippets will resolve and render their contents prior to await render(...) returning.” A boundary on the server catches only what is thrown inside it, and a script is not inside anything, so a refusal there refuses the whole render.

So the await moved into the boundary as well. It is {const result = $derived(await query)}, the first of the declaration tags quoted above, and the script keeps only the request. A remote query is a promise and an object at once, which is what makes the split work. The script creates it, the markup awaits it, and a button can refresh it.

The pending snippet had to go with it, and it had been costing something all along. “During server-side rendering, a boundary with a pending snippet renders that snippet and ignores the rest of its content.” The server had been waiting for the query, because the script told it to, and then sending “Running…” where the rows should have been. Without the snippet, the server renders what the boundary holds: the result when the query answers, and the failed snippet when it refuses, because in SvelteKit 3 errors thrown during rendering are “routed through handleError and then passed to the nearest error boundary” — on the server as well as in the browser.

Why the response is still a 400

SvelteKit gives the response the status of the error a boundary caught while it rendered, and here that is the checker’s 400. Forcing a 200 would be a small lie. A link to a query the server refuses is a bad request, and the status is what a load balancer, a crawler and this product’s own access log read. The person in front of the page gets the same fact as a sentence, next to the query they can fix.

The caught error also becomes page.error, and page.status follows it — when the server renders, and again in the browser for every refusal a boundary catches — and neither is cleared when the next run succeeds. Nothing in Sextant reads them. Copy this pattern into an app whose layout does, and it will believe it is showing an error page long after it is not: on a page with boundaries like these, page.error means “a boundary caught something”, not “this route failed”.

A first repair kept the await in the script and caught the refusal there as a value, to throw it again inside the boundary. It worked, at the price of a wrapper type, a function that threw on purpose and an effect that watched every answer to reset the boundary — and the server still sent “Running…”. Moving one await replaced all of it.

The same await on three more pages

The traces list, the trace page and the alerts list had all awaited their queries in the script, each with a pending snippet in its boundary. In the browser that held up, because each read its result only in the markup. On the server it was the explore page’s waste exactly: the server waited for the query, then sent “Loading…” in its place, and with JavaScript off the page said “Loading…” for good. Each got the same fix — the await inside the boundary as a declaration tag, and no pending.

The alerts page needed one more line. Its rule form sits outside the boundary and used to name a rule’s type as (typeof list)[number]; with list declared inside the boundary, the type is named from the query instead: type Rule = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof rules>>[number].

The settings page keeps its pending snippets, and that is the same rule applied the other way. Its two lists were awaited in the markup already, inside boundaries that have a pending snippet, so the server never runs those queries at all: it sends “Loading…” and the browser asks once it is awake. What was wrong on the other pages was paying for both: the server waited for the data, sent it along in the page’s payload for the browser, and drew “Loading…” instead of it. Either draw it, or do not ask for it; chapter 43 has the settings lists.

The drawer keeps its pending snippet, on purpose, and the reason is where it is drawn. It exists only in the browser, opened from page.state, so the server’s way with pending never comes into it — and with the await inside the boundary, the drawer opens at once and says it is loading. In the script, that snippet had never shown: a component’s own await is waited for by whatever boundary holds the component, not by the boundaries it draws, so the drawer appeared only once the trace had arrived.

A boundary for each run

A boundary that has failed then has to be drawn again. Its content is gone, so nothing in it is waiting for the next answer. Svelte has a block for exactly this: key blocks “destroy and recreate their contents when the value of an expression changes”. Keyed on the run — the query, the range and which press of Run asked — the results area is a new boundary for every run. The old area stays on screen while the new one waits for its answer, because Svelte keeps a block’s new content out of the page until its await has settled, and then the two change places — rows, or the next refusal.

The first version was keyed on query, and the tab froze when two runs overlapped. The remote-functions documentation says that queries “are cached while they’re on the page, meaning getPosts() === getPosts()”, and in SvelteKit 3.1.0 the client does not do that: each call makes a new object in front of the shared cache entry. With two runs in flight, each read of the key found a new object and started the block over, without end. A string built from the arguments is equal to itself.

Run always asks, and says so

Run sends a request every time, even when the query on screen is the one in the editor. A range like -6h means something new every minute, and an area that failed for a passing reason — a dropped connection, an expired session — can only be drawn again from a fresh answer. The client keeps a query’s last answer for as long as the query is on the page, so the new area would be drawn from the old answer without the refresh(). Each press also counts as a new run, so even the same question gets an area of its own.

Why “Running…” needs tick() and settled()

Because Svelte keeps the old rows up on purpose. “When an await expression depends on a particular piece of state, changes to that state will not be reflected in the UI until the asynchronous work has completed”, and a status changed in the same update is held back with it, appearing only once there is nothing left to wait for. $effect.pending() cannot see it either: it counts the promises “pending in the current boundary, not including child boundaries”, and the run’s await is in the next area, a boundary not yet on the page. So the count goes up in an update of its own, and tick() lets it paint — in the documentation’s words, “without this, the change to updating will be grouped with the other changes, meaning it won’t be reflected in the UI” — and settled(), which “resolves when the current update is complete”, says when to take it down. The status is a live region that is always there and only sometimes has words in it, so a screen reader already knows it when “Running…” arrives; the results say aria-busy while they wait.

Trying again

“Try again” is a run of the query on screen, not of whatever is now in the editor, so it shares everything above: a fresh answer, a new area, the refusal kept up until the answer is in. What it adds is the focus. The area it sits in is replaced by its own answer, so the button that was pressed is gone afterwards, and focus on a removed element falls back to the page body. Somebody pressing it with a keyboard was thrown to the top of the page after every try.

Why the focus is handed back after settled()

Each area offers an element for the focus through an attachment — the results section, which has tabindex="-1" so it can be focused without becoming a stop for Tab, or the new “Try again”. The first attempt had that element focus itself as it was attached, and the test that held the keyboard on a refusal failed: “Expected: focused, Received: inactive”. The rows case passed and the refusal did not, which gave it away. Svelte builds the next area out of sight and swaps it in once its await has settled, and a failed snippet is drawn the moment the refusal arrives — before the swap — so the button was focusing itself while it was not yet in the document, and the browser ignores that. After settled(), whichever area the answer drew is on the page.

While a run is waiting, the button is aria-disabled rather than disabled. A disabled button gives up the keyboard focus that just pressed it, before there is anywhere for the focus to go.

Tests for every way a refusal arrives

With JavaScript off, the screen is only what the server sent, which is where this half of the bug lived. Run against three earlier pages, the same test fails for three different reasons, and together they show why it looks at the page as well as the status — down to the editor, with the query in it.

Two more tests use the live page: a link opens with the query in the editor, ready to fix, and a reload after a refused Run lands on the same explanation. The rest hold requests back, or cut them off. The first presses “Try again” with the keyboard on a refusal that will come back the same: it proves a request is made, that the refusal stays up and the page says it is running while it waits, and that the focus ends on the new button.

The second is the case the button exists for. It cuts the connection, runs a query, and expects the client hook’s sentence from chapter 41 in place of “Internal Error”; then it puts the connection back, presses “Try again”, and expects the rows, with the focus on them.

The last two hold answers back. One presses Run on the query already on screen and expects a request, “Running…” and aria-busy while it waits, and the old rows kept up until the new ones land. The other lets two runs’ answers go at once and expects the second one’s rows — the test that froze on the key made from query.

Checkpoint

  • A results table draws forty sparklines in one round trip.
  • Your rule form works with JavaScript disabled.
  • An invalid rule shows a message beside the field rather than an error page.
  • A toggle the server refuses goes back to how it was and says why.
  • A query the server refuses is explained where its rows would be, with the editor still there.
  • A link to a refused query opens the explore page with the reason, the editor and a 400, even with JavaScript off.
  • The traces, a trace and the alert rules are in the server’s HTML, not “Loading…”.
  • Run asks the server every time, and says “Running…” until the answer is drawn.
  • “Try again” after a dropped connection draws the rows, and leaves the keyboard on them.
  • Two runs pressed in quick succession end on the answer to the second.
